title: 'Penang’s draft plan could open more of its hills to building
body: 'Kam Suan Pheng and Evelyn Teh “Rising from the sea in that first light of dawn that touches reality with a gentle charm, the Penang hills provide an unforgettable landmark for the visitor sailing in by sea. From the palm-fringed bays as yet a black indistinguishable smudge, the eye follows the flowing silhouette of the hills.” – Margaret Khor, The Straits Times Annual, 1960. Ask anyone who has crossed on the ferry, or driven over the bridge at dusk, and they will say the same: that green line of hills is how you know you are home. That silhouette is part of what makes Penang, Penang. Beyond the scenery, the hills are part of the island’s natural public infrastructure – one that is rarely counted. They hold soil, absorb and direct water, support forests and wildlife, and shape the landscape where we and our ancestors have lived. That landscape could change significantly if the draft State Structure Plan 2040 is adopted without stronger safeguards for hill and slope development. First, some background. The current Penang State Structure Plan 2030 does not allow development on land 76 metres (250 feet) or more above sea level, or on slopes of 25 degrees or steeper. There are limited exceptions for infrastructure and utilities. The limit is stricter than the national guideline. The state set it because it recognised how fragile, and how important, the island’s hills are. - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member The 2030 plan reads: Sebarang Pembangunan Perbandaran Yang Meliputi Pembangunan Skim Perumahan Perhotelan Resort Perdagangan Perindustrian Dan Sebarang Struktur Bangunan Footprint Tidak Dibenarkan Di Kawasan:- - Kawasan Tanah Tinggi Yang Diwartakan Di Bawah Akta Pemeliharaan Tanah 1960 Akta 385 Atau - Sebarang Tanah Yang Berada Pada Aras 76 meter 250 kaki) Ke Atas Atau - Kawasan Berkecerunan 25 Darjah Ke Atas KECUALI Bagi Pemajuan Infrastruktur Dan Utiliti Dibenarkan Dengan Syarat Syarat Dari Jabatan Teknikal Yang Berkaitan Dan Mendapat Kelulusan Dari Pihak Berkuasa Negeri. In English: Any urban development, including housing schemes, hotels, resorts, commercial or industrial developments, and any building structures, is prohibited in the following areas: - Highland areas gazetted under the Land Conservation Act 1960 (Act 385); or - Any land situated at an elevation of 76 metres (250 feet) or higher; or - Areas with a slope gradient of 25 degrees or steeper; EXCEPT for infrastructure and utility developments, which are permitted subject to conditions imposed by relevant technical departments and approval from the State Authority. The key concern The state government rolled out a new draft 2040 plan in August – years before 2030 arrives. It will overwrite the previous version. The draft 2040 plan says: Strategi Perancangan PS3-1: Pembangunan di Kawasan Khusus yang Melebihi Ketinggian 76 meter. Strategi ini merupakan pendekatan perancangan yang memberi kelonggaran kawalan ketinggian bangunan secara terpilih di kawasan khas yang telah dikenal pasti sebagai kawasan tumpuan pembangunan strategik. Pelaksanaan strategi ini bertujuan mengoptimumkan penggunaan tanah yang terhad melalui pembangunan berintensiti tinggi dan berorientasikan transit, khususnya di pusat bandar, koridor ekonomi dan kawasan pesisir yang mempunyai kapasiti infrastruktur mencukupi. Walau bagaimanapun, kebenaran ini tertakluk kepada penilaian teknikal terperinci seperti kesesuaian guna tanah, nisbah plot, kawalan kepadatan, impak trafik, keselamatan, impak visual serta pematuhan kepada garis panduan reka bentuk bandar dan kajian impak alam sekitar. In English: Planning Strategy PS3-1: Development in Special Areas Exceeding a Height of 76 Metres. This strategy is a planning approach that allows for selective flexibility regarding building height controls in specific areas identified as strategic development hubs. Its implementation aims to optimize limited land use through high-intensity, transit-oriented development, particularly in city centres, economic corridors and coastal areas with adequate infrastructure capacity. However, such approval is subject to detailed technical assessments covering aspects such as land-use suitability, plot ratio, density controls, traffic impact, safety, visual impact, and compliance with urban design guidelines and environmental impact studies. In plain terms, the 2040 draft swaps ‘don’t build there’ (in the 2030 plan) for ‘build there if the paperwork says it’s safe’. The 2030 plan took a precautionary approach: keep away from the risk altogether. The 2040 draft replaces it with case-by-case approval, where each project’s own technical studies decide whether a hill can take it. Are these adequate safeguards, or is this a problem waiting to happen? Why change the limit? The threshold of 76m above sea level was not arbitrary. It was a deliberate safeguard that Penang chose to keep. Penang had adopted stricter controls than the national KSAS (environmentally sensitive areas) elevation framework, which it is now reverting to. The Safety Guideline for Hillsite Development (second edition, 2020) says Penang Island covers roughly 285 sq km. About 40% of it is Class 3 and Class 4 land, with slopes steeper than 25 degrees. The first version of the guideline went further. It reduced the footprint of buildings on hill land to make slopes safer and keep more green areas. Now these precautions are set aside. The 2040 draft presents this as a development strategy, not as a finding that the 76m limit is irrelevant. Outside the draft, no new evidence, assessment or policy review shows that the precautionary approach is no longer needed. What evidence, then, supports such a significant change in risk management? Look closely at the numbers. The highest point in Penang is 833m above sea level, but the horizontal area of the hills is small. The slopes are therefore compressed into a limited range of height and width. Add the complex pattern of hills and ridges, and very few pockets of land are flat enough to build on without cutting into the surrounding slopes. Even if building is allowed on isolated pockets, the roads needed to reach them must cross steeper terrain. Their environmental impact will reach far beyond the site. We do not have to imagine what that looks like. In October 2017, a landslide at a construction site in Tanjung Bungah killed 11 workers. A year later, part of a ‘paired road’ at Bukit Kukus collapsed during construction, killing nine. Bukit Kukus was a road, exactly the kind of infrastructure the 2030 plan already allowed as an exception. If the exception alone could cost so many lives, what happens when the rule itself is lifted? This is probably why past planners chose the 76m (250ft) limit. That wisdom applies even more today, as climate change brings heavier and more frequent rain to fragile hills. And what happens on the hill does not stay on the hill. These slopes feed the Air Itam and Teluk Bahang dams that fill our taps. When forests can no longer hold the rain, it runs down into lowland streets as flash floods. One does not need to live on a hill to pay for what happens on one. Paperwork is not landscape planning Some may argue that a technical assessment before approval is a reasonable safeguard. It can tell us whether a project meets existing standards. These include the Penang Safety Guideline for Hill Site Development 2020, the EIA Guidelines for Development in Slope and Hill Areas issued by the Department of Environment, and the planning and management guide for environmentally sensitive areas by PLANMalaysia. But none of these answers the bigger question: how many projects can these hills absorb before the whole system gives way? The 2040 draft says hill development control is strengthened through risk assessment, including the environment’s carrying capacity and climate resilience. Any development on hill land between 300 and 1,200 metres, or between 150 and 300 metres, and on slopes above 25 degrees, must submit a geotechnical risk assessment and a climate risk assessment. However, we know of no publicly accessible study or official database that gathers the information needed as a baseline. This should be established before the first hill or slope proposal is submitted. It seems the draft simply adopted a guideline written for the highlands of the peninsula – not one drawn up for Penang island. Could we, or should we? With today’s engineering, there are many ways to stabilise a slope: retaining walls, modern drainage, soil nails, piles and engineered slopes. A project may well be shown to be safe on paper. But the natural slope will have been substantially altered. Its long-term safety then rests on things no approval can guarantee. These include construction quality, drainage maintenance, inspection, the capacity and funding of the agencies responsible, extreme weather and future changes in land use. The irony is that a retaining wall is only as safe as the last time someone cleared its drains. There is also no baseline of existing conditions or of the role the hills play. That role covers the watershed, ecological corridors, natural drainage and geological formations. Penang lacks a hill and slope master plan that understands how sensitive and connected the hills are. Only such a plan can properly define, map and measure the hills’ carrying capacity, including projected climate scenarios. So the question shifts. We could make hill and slope development safe. But should we, and at what cost, when we have no baseline data and no guarantee these projects will stay safe in the long term? A project being technically safe is not the same as the landscape being safe. Gazette first, assess later When a gazetted state structure plan marks an area as potentially developable, the effects ripple out quickly. Land values rise, investors form expectations, land changes hands, proposals are drawn up and contracts are signed. All of this happens long before any environmental impact or technical assessment is complete. That order of events tilts the outcome. Once money and contracts are committed, rejecting a project on environmental grounds carries legal and financial consequences. The seemingly rational way out is to reduce every risk to an ‘acceptable’ level and hope nothing goes wrong later. The assessment no longer decides whether to build, only how. Show us the evidence The 2040 draft marks a significant shift from precautionary restriction towards risk-based conditional development. That may be reasonable in some circumstances. But the draft must show why the previous limits are no longer needed. It must also explain how project-by-project checks will deal with risks that build up across the landscape, worsen with climate change and cannot be undone once a hill is cut. If Penang is deliberately moving beyond the precautionary framework to create more development opportunities, it should show us the evidence. That means the thresholds and landscape-level safeguards that justify the change, in the form of a hill and slope development master plan, published before the 2040 plan is gazetted, not after. In the end, for most of us, this is not really a debate about slope angles, geotechnical reports or even the state structure plan. It is about the hills we know, some of us since childhood. These are the hills we see from our windows, or on the drive home after a long day at work. On them lie the green trails we climb at weekends to take in the view of our beloved Penang from above. It is also about feeling safe when the torrential rain comes. Can we sleep soundly knowing the hills near us will keep doing what they have always done: holding the soil, soaking up the water and slowing the runoff before it reaches our neighbourhoods? Or will we rely more and more on concrete walls and drains to protect us from hills we ourselves have altered? Dr Kam Suan Pheng is a soil scientist and co-founder of Penang Hills Watch, with a doctorate in agronomy-soil from Cornell University. Evelyn Teh is a Penang-based public policy researcher and environmental scientist specialising in ecological management, climate change and urban studies. title: 'Cover Story: Banks shift tokenisation into higher gear
body: 'Cover Story: Banks shift tokenisation into higher gear This article first appeared in Wealth, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 28, 2026 - October 4, 2026 Tokenisation, the act of representing an asset or claim as a token on a distributed ledger or blockchain, has remained under the radar among local financial institutions. Until recently. The catalyst, market observers say, came from Bank Negara Malaysia, when it launched the Digital Asset Innovation Hub (DAIH) in June 2025 and published its discussion paper on asset tokenisation in the Malaysian financial sector in October 2025. The public feedback window for the discussion paper closed on March 1, 2026, and Bank Negara hosted its third Asset Tokenisation Industry Working Group session in August this year. The discussion paper states that proof-of-concepts and live pilots will be conducted in a controlled environment through the DAIH this year, with testing expected to continue into 2027, alongside the compilation and publication of findings and the evaluation of key insights. Three banks have launched initiatives under the DAIH. The banks are under CIMB Group Holdings Bhd (KL:CIMB); Standard Chartered Bank Malaysia Bhd (Standard Chartered Malaysia), together with Capital A Bhd (KL:CAPITALA); and Malayan Banking Bhd (KL:MAYBANK). Chu Kok Wei, CEO of group wholesale banking and corporate treasurer at CIMB Group, says Malaysian banks are not the earliest to embrace the technology, but they have been moving fast recently. “We might be the country that’s moving at the fastest speed in Southeast Asia in the last one year, based on my observation, by looking at all the stakeholders and our experience and conversation with regulators,” he says. His observation coincides with the findings of HSBC’s Redefining Treasury in Asia Pacific 2026: Voices of Treasury report, published on Sept 17. The report notes that Malaysia stands out as the most enthusiastic market in the region on digital currency adoption, with 50% of respondents saying they were very likely to use digital currencies in the next two years, far higher than the regional average of 19%. Digital currency is tokenised money, which can take the form of tokenised deposits, stablecoins or central bank digital currency. Nasdaq has also received the Securities and Exchange Commission’s (SEC) approval to enable certain stocks and ETFs to be issued, traded and settled in tokenised form. “These organisations are not crypto-native firms pushing blockchain, but some of the oldest and largest financial institutions adopting new infrastructure,” according to Citi. On Sept 17, the SEC unveiled its long-awaited exemption that will allow companies to offer trading in blockchain-based or “tokenised” stocks and other securities. Four days later, the European Central Bank launched preparatory work to invest a small portion of its own fund in tokenised securities, enabling it to gain practical experience as an investor and build institutional expertise in the use of distributed ledger technology in financial markets. Put simply, a tokenised deposit is a form of digital money that is transferred and settled on a secure blockchain or distributed ledger, rather than through traditional payment infrastructure such as PayNet’s Real-time Retail Payments Platform (RPP) or Bank Negara’s RENTAS+. Of the total issuance, RM1.38 billion was represented in tokenised form and subscribed by 12 institutional investors. Both legs of the transaction — CIMB’s tokenised sukuk and the tokenised deposits used to pay for them — were settled on the bank’s own blockchain, CIMB Blockchain Connect. “Khazanah’s tokenised sukuk pilot project was RM100 million with a one-year tenure. The transaction was carried out in partnership with Virtual Economy Technology Sdn Bhd (V System) via its tokenisation platform, NexA. Earlier, on March 30, the bank successfully completed the first transaction of its tokenised deposits and cross-border payments with energy infrastructure company Yinson Holdings Bhd (KL:YINSON). The project integrates the tokenisation of bank deposits with an on-chain foreign exchange (FX) conversion of ringgit to Singapore dollars, and a subsequent cross-border payment between the two countries in near real-time, using Maybank’s permissioned blockchain. “Our focus is on turning tokenisation from concept into real-world applications,” says Tan. Maybank Singapore has also joined the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s BLOOM initiative, an industry project to improve cross-border payments using tokenised bank liabilities and regulated stablecoins through an interoperable digital financial system. On the ringgit stablecoin initiative for B2B settlement with Capital A, Standard Chartered Malaysia interim CEO, head of coverage and chief financial officer Mushahid Syed says: “It is still in an initial testing phase. We will share further details subject to approval from Bank Negara.” In his email response, Mushahid Syed adds that the bank’s focus is on connecting tokenised assets to the wider ecosystem, including digital money, custody, trading, collateral and settlement infrastructure. “This includes exploring how digital forms of money can interact more seamlessly with tokenised assets, enabling more efficient access to yield-bearing investment products, and how these tokenised assets themselves can be used as collateral across the financial ecosystem,” he says. Trading tokenised bonds and sukuk on the blockchain While not spelling out the bank’s next step on its tokenisation initiative, CIMB’s Chu says market players would expect the trading of CIMB’s tokenised sukuk on the blockchain. “We started with the issuance of tokenised securities. Bonds and sukuk being a tradable instrument, naturally, industry players would look at how we can trade these tokenised securities more efficiently [on the blockchain] and start to harness the benefits of it,” he says. Halogen Capital, the country’s first digital asset manager, is one of the institutions that subscribed to CIMB’s tokenised sukuk. Its founder and CEO Hann Liew echoes Chu’s view. “We purchased one lot of CIMB tokenised sukuk, and CIMB gives us access to view the tokens. There’s an online platform where institutional investors like us can log in and see our holdings. Put simply, it is like CIMB Octo for retail users, where you can log in and see your details. “However, the challenge is the next step, which is to enable active on-chain trading of the sukuk, which isn’t yet live. Can we see transactions that happened on the blockchain? Can we conduct analysis and trade on it?” he says. One might ask how it is different when tokenised sukuk is traded on the blockchain. Chu points to several key features, including instant settlement, round-the-clock trading and fractionalisation. With a distributed ledger shared across various parties, a trade executed on the blockchain can be settled almost instantaneously — otherwise known as “atomic settlement” — which reduces settlement risk. Settlement risk is the danger that the money is paid but the securities are not delivered, or vice versa. A classic example dates back to 1974, when banks globally paid Deutsche marks to German lender Herstatt Bank in the morning but did not receive the US dollars they expected later in the day. Herstatt had made wrong directional bets on the greenback and was shut down by regulators midday, with the value of transactions left unsettled estimated at US$200 million. Settlement risk becomes severe when large sums are involved. Meanwhile, when trades can be matched, settled and recorded automatically and efficiently, bonds and sukuk can be traded round the clock, translating into cost savings and a potentially more vibrant market. Tokenised securities and deposits are programmable, which is where smart contracts come into play. A smart contract is code on a blockchain that automatically carries out the terms of an agreement when conditions are met, without human intervention. Chu says smart contracts can be used for market events. For instance, where a bond or sukuk pays a coupon every six months, the profit can be distributed automatically via the distributed ledger. “All these are baby steps that we are taking, from the primary market to secondary, and eventually it covers even redemptions,” he says. Tokenised securities can be fractionalised, which opens up the possibility of tokenised bonds and sukuk becoming easily accessible to retail investors at a much lower amount. But Chu says tokenisation and blockchain are merely a technological enabler; further democratisation of bonds and sukuk would require changes in rules and regulations. “We all need to kind of contain our excitement about how tokenisation enables retail participation for now. It provides a platform, but suitability for investors, fair disclosure [of information] and all other relevant processes have to be continuously assessed by the regulators,” he says. Interoperability between blockchains, and between the new and old systems Against such a backdrop, tokenisation initiatives undertaken by local banks are based on the “digital twin” concept, which means the on-chain token mirrors the traditional legal records rather than replacing them. “From a legal sense, digital twin means the whole process of the issuance of CIMB sukuk follows existing rules and regulations and contract. The original contract remains valid, while the digital token is only a replica. In this case, you don’t need to answer what is the relationship of the replica and the underlying assets,” says Chu. However, the country’s rules and regulations will need to change if financial services were to move fully onto the blockchain, which is one of the challenges in tokenisation. Chu says other challenges include interoperability, which means the deployment of digital tokens across the different blockchains of different banks. However, he says CIMB prefers to focus on something else: the interoperability between the new technology, which is the blockchain, and the existing ones, especially in the bond market. “This is much more important as bonds and sukuk are an established asset class with a total value of more than RM2 trillion in the system. How can these assets slowly evolve over time, so that people can embrace the new ones [issued with the new technology] without feeling that the old ones are out of fashion? “This is extremely important, as institutional fund managers can be holding a 30-year bond today. There are many 30-year bonds out there and they start to worry about what happens if all these are going to be tokenised,” he says. Maybank’s Tan agrees that beyond technology and process design, the successful deployment of tokenisation also depends on many other factors, including interoperability, regulatory alignment and broader industry adoption. From a practical perspective, a key challenge lies in integrating tokenised solutions into existing systems, processes and operating models, he adds. This means a bank needs to stay forward-looking and rethink workflows from the ground up, including what should be retained, rebuilt, simplified or, in some cases, fundamentally redesigned to realise the full benefits of tokenisation. “Realising the full potential of tokenisation will require close collaboration among regulators, financial institutions and technology providers to establish common standards and trusted market infrastructure,” says Tan. Standard Chartered Malaysia’s Mushahid Syed adds that developing digital infrastructure that offers accessible, cost-effective and instant alternative wholesale payments is key for a trading nation like Malaysia, with its strong small and medium enterprise base. There is little doubt that tokenisation, underpinned by blockchain technology, will make banking and financial services more efficient and effective when it matures. Workflows, organisational structures and the content of certain jobs may evolve. Changes are already afoot. “An example I always tell everyone is that we are now using iPhone 18, which has evolved significantly from its first version. The same applies to the evolution of the financial services industry and the role of people working in it,” says Chu. Save by subscribing to us for your print and/or digital copy. title: 'AHB KEKALKAN AGIHAN PENDAPATAN LIMA SEN SEUNIT BAGI TAHUN KEWANGAN 2026 – Gerbangpost.com
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR,. Amanah Hartanah Bumiputera (AHB) mengekalkan agihan pendapatan sebanyak lima sen seunit bagi tahun kewangan berakhir 30 Sept 2026, yang KUALA LUMPUR,. Amanah Hartanah Bumiputera (AHB) mengekalkan agihan pendapatan sebanyak lima sen seunit bagi tahun kewangan berakhir 30 Sept 2026, yang memberi manfaat kepada lebih 82,000 pemegang unit. Pelaburan Hartanah Bhd (PHB) bersama pengurus dananya, PHB Asset Management Bhd (PHBAM), berkata agihan pendapatan akhir bagi tempoh enam bulan berakhir 30 Sept 2026 adalah sebanyak 2.1 sen seunit, dengan tambahan agihan bonus sebanyak 0.4 sen seunit yang diisytiharkan PHB selaku penaja dana itu. “Edaran bonus itu akan diberikan bagi 1,000,000 unit pertama bagi setiap pemegang unit. Dengan mengambil kira agihan pendapatan interim sebanyak 2.5 sen seunit yang diisytiharkan pada April 2026, jumlah keseluruhan agihan pendapatan AHB bagi tahun kewangan berakhir 2026 adalah lima sen seunit,” menurut kenyataan itu. PHB berkata sebanyak RM120.13 juta akan diagihkan pada pusingan akhir, menjadikan jumlah keseluruhan agihan tahunan sebanyak RM236.41 juta. Pengarah Urusan kumpulan PHB Mazuki Abdullah @ Muhammad berkata agihan pendapatan bagi setahun penuh itu mencerminkan daya tahan AHB yang berterusan serta kekuatan portfolio hartanah asasnya, disokong pendekatan pengurusan aset dan pelaburan yang berdisiplin oleh PHB. “Prestasi AHB tahun ini membuktikan komitmen kami untuk terus memberikan pulangan yang kompetitif kepada pemegang unit. “Pada masa sama, kami kekal memberi tumpuan kepada usaha memperkukuh kedudukan AHB sebagai instrumen pelaburan pilihan pelabur Bumiputera menerusi pengurusan modal yang berhemat, strategi pelaburan yang dinamik serta pengoptimuman portfolio yang berterusan bagi memastikan pertumbuhan yang mampan danpenciptaan nilai jangka panjang,” katanya. Sementara itu, Ketua Pegawai Eksekutif PHBAM Zulkifli Ishak berkata pengurus dana itu kekal fokus menguruskan AHB secara bertanggungjawab bagi memastikan dana berkenaan terus menjadi pilihan pelaburan yang mudah diakses oleh pelabur Bumiputera. PHB berkata agihan pendapatan itu akan dibayar dalam bentuk unit AHB yang dikreditkan terus ke dalam akaun AHB pemegang unit selewat-lewatnya pada 13 Okt 2026. Agihan tersebut akan dilaburkan semula secara automatik, sekali gus membolehkan pemegang unit menambah pegangan unit serta berpotensi menikmati kesan pengkompaunan dalam jangka panjang. “Pelabur Bumiputera yang ingin melanggan AHB boleh berbuat demikian pada harga tetap RM1 seunit, dengan pelaburan minimum RM100 dan maksimum RM1 juta. “Langganan boleh dibuat melalui cawangan pengedar yang sah di seluruh negara, iaitu Malayan Banking Bhd (Maybank), AmBank Bhd, AmBank Islamic Bhd, Bank Islam Malaysia Bhd dan Bank Kerjasama Rakyat Malaysia Bhd,” katanya. — BERNAMA

Amanah Hartanah Bumiputera (AHB) mengekalkan agihan pendapatan sebanyak lima sen seunit bagi tahun kewangan berakhir 30 Sept 2026, yang KUALA LUMPUR,. Amanah Hartanah Bumiputera (AHB) mengekalkan agihan pendapatan sebanyak lima sen seunit bagi tahun kewangan berakhir 30 Sept 2026, yang memberi manfaat kepada lebih 82,000 pemegang unit. Pelaburan Hartanah Bhd (PHB) bersama pengurus dananya, PHB Asset Management Bhd (PHBAM), berkata agihan pendapatan akhir bagi tempoh enam bulan berakhir 30 Sept 2026 adalah sebanyak 2.1 sen seunit, dengan tambahan agihan bonus sebanyak 0.4 sen seunit yang diisytiharkan PHB selaku penaja dana itu. “Edaran bonus itu akan diberikan bagi 1,000,000 unit pertama bagi setiap pemegang unit. Dengan mengambil kira agihan pendapatan interim sebanyak 2.5 sen seunit yang diisytiharkan pada April 2026, jumlah keseluruhan agihan pendapatan AHB bagi tahun kewangan berakhir 2026 adalah lima sen seunit,” menurut kenyataan itu. PHB berkata sebanyak RM120.13 juta akan diagihkan pada pusingan akhir, menjadikan jumlah keseluruhan agihan tahunan sebanyak RM236.41 juta. Pengarah Urusan kumpulan PHB Mazuki Abdullah @ Muhammad berkata agihan pendapatan bagi setahun penuh itu mencerminkan daya tahan AHB yang berterusan serta kekuatan portfolio hartanah asasnya, disokong pendekatan pengurusan aset dan pelaburan yang berdisiplin oleh PHB. “Prestasi AHB tahun ini membuktikan komitmen kami untuk terus memberikan pulangan yang kompetitif kepada pemegang unit. “Pada masa sama, kami kekal memberi tumpuan kepada usaha memperkukuh kedudukan AHB sebagai instrumen pelaburan pilihan pelabur Bumiputera menerusi pengurusan modal yang berhemat, strategi pelaburan yang dinamik serta pengoptimuman portfolio yang berterusan bagi memastikan pertumbuhan yang mampan danpenciptaan nilai jangka panjang,” katanya. Sementara itu, Ketua Pegawai Eksekutif PHBAM Zulkifli Ishak berkata pengurus dana itu kekal fokus menguruskan AHB secara bertanggungjawab bagi memastikan dana berkenaan terus menjadi pilihan pelaburan yang mudah diakses oleh pelabur Bumiputera. PHB berkata agihan pendapatan itu akan dibayar dalam bentuk unit AHB yang dikreditkan terus ke dalam akaun AHB pemegang unit selewat-lewatnya pada 13 Okt 2026. Agihan tersebut akan dilaburkan semula secara automatik, sekali gus membolehkan pemegang unit menambah pegangan unit serta berpotensi menikmati kesan pengkompaunan dalam jangka panjang. “Pelabur Bumiputera yang ingin melanggan AHB boleh berbuat demikian pada harga tetap RM1 seunit, dengan pelaburan minimum RM100 dan maksimum RM1 juta. “Langganan boleh dibuat melalui cawangan pengedar yang sah di seluruh negara, iaitu Malayan Banking Bhd (Maybank), AmBank Bhd, AmBank Islamic Bhd, Bank Islam Malaysia Bhd dan Bank Kerjasama Rakyat Malaysia Bhd,” katanya. — BERNAMA

title: 'Bursa Malaysia Ends Lower as It Tracks Cautious Wall Street Performance
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 1 – Bursa Malaysia closed lower on Thursday, October 1, 2026, under persistent selling pressure across major blue-chip counters, tracking a mixed and cautious overnight performance on Wall Street. The benchmark FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) fell 20.81 points, or 1.26 per cent, to finish at 1,630.36, down from Wednesday’s close of 1,651.17. After opening 1.30 points weaker at 1,649.87, the key index fluctuated between an intraday low of 1,630.10 and a high of 1,649.87 throughout the trading session. Market breadth was negative as decliners outpaced gainers 750 to 342, with 495 counters trading unchanged, 1,186 untraded, and 12 suspended. Total market turnover dropped to 3.1 billion units valued at RM2.7 billion, compared to 3.63 billion units worth RM3.62 billion recorded on Wednesday. Economic data released earlier in the day showed that the S&P Global Malaysia Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) slipped into contraction territory, falling to 49.9 in September from 50.2 in August—marking the first downturn in operating conditions in four months. Regionally, the S&P Global ASEAN Manufacturing PMI also eased to 52.1 in September from 52.3 in August. Blue-Chip Heavyweights and Active Counters Financial, utility, and healthcare heavyweights experienced notable selling pressure: - CIMB dropped 10 sen to RM7.69. - IHH Healthcare erased 13 sen to RM7.70. - Tenaga Nasional lost 6 sen to RM12.90. - Maybank slipped 4 sen to RM9.95. - Public Bank fell 3 sen to RM4.67. In active trading, ACE Market debutant GB Bond slumped 4.5 sen to close at 20.5 sen. Jaks Resources dropped 2.5 sen to 18 sen, and VS Industry dipped 1 sen to 27 sen. Meanwhile, Zetrix AI and HHRG each added half a sen to close at 16.5 sen. Top gainers for the session were led by technology and consumer stocks: - Malaysian Pacific Industries: Surged 72 sen to RM41.12. - Ayer Holdings: Advanced 20 sen to RM7.70. - Riverview Rubber Estates: Rose 12 sen to RM3.02. - Dutch Lady Malaysia Industries: Added 10 sen to RM30.00. - Vitrox: Gained 9 sen to RM10.00. Plantation and consumer-linked counters featured among the session’s major losers: - Kuala Lumpur Kepong: Led losses, dropping 78 sen to RM21.42. - Allianz Malaysia: Declined 62 sen to RM21.00. - United Plantations: Shed 60 sen to RM30.96. - Fraser & Neave & Hong Leong Industries: Each fell 32 sen to RM21.42 and RM16.14, respectively. –NMT

body: '银行股突遭抛售潮 马股重摔至今年新低！ （吉隆坡7日讯）银行股再次遭到抛售，拖累马股今早开市不久便面临沉重卖压，早盘一度暴跌超过18点或1.1%，不仅失守1630点关卡，还创下今年来新低。 富马隆综指今早以1633.54点迎市，随着银行股陷入沉重卖压，早盘一度重挫18.54点至1614.81点，写下今年来新低，同时也是去年12月以来最低。 截至早上11时，隆综指跌16.16点或0.99%至1617.19点，成交量有5亿4777万2000股。 银行股今日齐聚下跌股榜，当中以联昌集团（CIMB，1023，主要板金服）卖压最重，早盘以7.7令吉迎市后不断探低，盘中低见7.35令吉，跌35仙或4.5%。 该股目前报7.37令吉，挫33仙或4.3%，成交量有1211万6600股，为全场第3大下跌股。 大盘料维持盘整 大马银行集团（AMBANK，1015，主要板金服）一度大跌4.2%至6.20令吉，丰隆银行（HLBANK，5819，主要板金服）则跌2.2%至21.60令吉。 马银行（MAYBANK，1155，主要板金服）早盘虽曾回升至10令吉，在仍不敌抛售潮，最新跌7仙至9.90令吉，暂有605万9200股易手。 丰隆投行研究指出，政府将在本周五（9日）提呈2027年财政预算案，而美国与伊朗紧张局势升温，加上美联储持续释放鹰派讯号，预计将令隆综指维持避险情绪下的盘整走势。 此外，在油价高企、债券收益率攀升，以及外资持续撤出的背景下，市场风险偏好料受压。 数据显示，截至周二（6日），外资净卖600万令吉的马股，已连续10个交易日从马股撤资；10月迄今累计净卖3亿4100万令吉，今年来净卖出达64亿9000万令吉。 散户在周二同样净卖4500万令吉，反观本地机构已连续五个交易日进场扶盘，昨日净买5100万令吉的马股。 The content is a snapshot from Publisher. body: '丰隆银行3分行明年关闭，客户业务转移至附近分行！ 丰隆银行（Hong Leong Bank）将关闭3家位于吉隆坡的分行，最后营业日定于2027年2月19日（星期五），受影响分行的客户及业务将转移至附近分行。 根据丰隆银行官网资料，3家即将关闭的分行分别位于Segambut、Brickfields及Pandan Indah。 3家分行将搬去哪？ 其中，Segambut分行关闭后，相关业务将转移至Menjalara分行；Brickfields分行的业务则转往Bangsar分行。 至于Pandan Indah分行，相关业务将转移至Ampang Taman Putra分行。 这意味着，受影响客户日后仍可继续通过丰隆银行其他分行办理相关业务，不过需要前往新的指定分行。 2月19日最后营业 上述3家分行的最后营业日为2027年2月19日（星期五）。 客户若平时习惯到这些分行办理银行业务，可留意相关安排，并在分行关闭后前往指定的替代分行。 银行也建议客户根据自身需要，提前熟悉新的服务地点，以免分行关闭后影响日常银行业务。 全国仍有逾200家分行 尽管这3家分行将关闭，丰隆银行在全国仍维持规模庞大的实体服务网络。 目前，丰隆银行在全国拥有超过200家分行及1025个自助服务机（ATM），客户仍可通过其他分行及自助服务渠道办理相关银行业务。 随着银行业持续推动数码化，越来越多客户通过网上银行及手机应用办理转账、缴费及其他日常银行业务，银行也持续根据客户使用情况调整实体分行网络。 因此，这次关闭3家分行主要涉及相关地点的服务网络调整，客户的银行账户及业务并不会因为分行关闭而终止。

title: 'Bursa Malaysia dibuka tinggi berikutan momentum positif Wall Street
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR: Bursa Malaysia dibuka tinggi pada Selasa, seiring dengan momentum positif Wall Street semalaman, memandangkan harga minyak yang terkawal susulan pemulihan eksport minyak mentah dari Asia Barat, mengimbangi trend penjualan berterusan dalam pasaran bon Perbendaharaan AS. Pada 9.10 pagi, FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) meningkat 7.14 mata atau 0.44 peratus kepada 1,638.89 berbanding paras 1,631.75 ketika ditutup pada Isnin. Indeks utama itu dibuka 4.63 mata lebih tinggi kepada 1,636.38. Sentimen pasaran secara keseluruhan positif dengan kaunter untung mengatasi kaunter rugi sebanyak 272 berbanding 202, sebanyak 364 kaunter tidak berubah, 1,944 tidak diniagakan dan 13 digantung dagangan. Jumlah dagangan berjumlah 440.19 juta saham bernilai RM164.76 juta. Malacca Securities Sdn Bhd memaklumkan bahawa prestasi positif Wall Street semalaman menyaksikan Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 dan Nasdaq Composite masing-masing meningkat sebanyak 0.2 peratus, 0.7 peratus dan 1.1 peratus, manakala harga minyak mentah Brent dan hasil Perbendaharaan 10 tahun masing-masing mencecah US$100.3 setong dan 5.3 peratus. "Di peringkat tempatan, kami menjangkakan pelabur akan terus bersikap selektif menjelang pengumuman Belanjawan 2027, dengan tumpuan diberikan kepada sektor-sektor yang berpotensi mendapat manfaat. "Syarikat-syarikat dalam sektor mekanikal dan elektrikal mungkin terus menyaksikan minat belian, disokong oleh penekanan kerajaan terhadap infrastruktur kecerdasan buatan (AI) serta projek tulang belakang Grid Nasional 500-kilovolt Tenaga Nasional Bhd, yang memberi kelebihan kepada syarikat seperti MN Holdings Bhd, Southern Cable Group Bhd dan Powerwell Holdings Bhd," menurut firma itu dalam nota penyelidikan hari ini. Selain itu, Malacca Securities menyatakan bahawa usaha mengurangkan air tanpa hasil (NRW) juga mungkin kekal menjadi tumpuan, berpotensi memberi manfaat kepada syarikat seperti ISF Group Bhd dan Ranhill Utilities Bhd. "Akhir sekali, 99 Speed Mart Retail mungkin menyaksikan minat belian baharu susulan jangkaan peruntukan bantuan pengguna lebih tinggi di bawah Sumbangan Asas Rahmah dan Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah," menurut kenyataan itu. Sementara itu, Naib Presiden Penyelidikan Ekuiti Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd, Thong Pak Leng berkata Wall Street ditutup lebih kukuh, dengan Nasdaq mencatatkan paras tertinggi baharu apabila pedagang memilih untuk tidak mempedulikan cabaran pasaran semasa dan sebaliknya menumpukan perhatian kepada saham berkaitan AI bagi mengimbangi kesan kenaikan hasil bon. "Untuk hari ini, kami menjangkakan indeks akan bergerak dalam julat 1,630-1,640 memandangkan pasaran saham tempatan mungkin bersedia untuk aktiviti pembelian saham pada harga rendah," katanya kepada Bernama. body: '13th PropertyGuru Asia Awards Malaysia with iProperty honours real estate excellence Top developers celebrated the 13th PropertyGuru Asia Awards Malaysia in partnership with iProperty, presented by Lim Soh & Goonting Advocates & Solicitors, at The St. Regis Kuala Lumpur. Guided by the theme “Defined by Excellence,” the 2026 PropertyGuru Asia Awards Malaysia with iProperty recognised the country’s best in real estate across 62 categories. From township developers to breakthrough companies, this year’s awards were comprehensive, honouring the best in different real estate segments and regions. Timber Land Group won the evening’s top honour, Best Developer, marking its first-ever win in the category, in addition to Best Developer (East Malaysia). CPI Land was named Best Developer (Central Malaysia) alongside award-winning project Tuan Straits. Tanah Sutera took both Best Developer (Southern Malaysia) and Best Landed Homes Developer, buoyed by winning project The Seed. JLand Group, named Best Township Developer, collected the most awards of any company, covering Developer, Development, and Design categories for projects including Arena Larkin; Bandar Tiram; Ibrahim Technopolis (IBTEC) – Aspiration Park; Ibrahim Technopolis (IBTEC) – STeP West; and Medora One. JRK Holdings Berhad won both Best Breakthrough Developer and Best Boutique Developer. Keck Seng (Malaysia) Berhad was named Best Mixed Use Developer, also winning for the project Daya 1 Residences, Taman Daya. Penang developers also made their mark at this year’s awards, with PTL Properties, Aspen and Pinnacle Group among the winners. PTL Properties was named Best Lifestyle Developer, with The Rimbun also winning Best Mass Market Landed Development (Northern) and Best Townhouse Development. Aspen’s Aspen Vision City received the Best Township Development (Northern) award, while Pinnacle Group won Best Premium High-Rise Development (Northern) for Pinnacle Bukit Gambier. Other companies with winning projects include Amalan Setar (M) Sdn Bhd, which won for Ixora Garden – Sari Alamanda 4 Phase 2; Armani Group (Armani Hallson Bukit Bintang); Astaka Kimlun Sdn Bhd (Amora Serviced Residence); BCB Land Sdn. Bhd. (Straya Heights); Coronade Properties Sdn Bhd (Coronation Square; Coronade Twins – Serviced Residences); CTC Development Malaysia Sdn Bhd (CTC Skyone @ Bukit Chagar); Faire Development (bée); Gunung Impian Development Sdn Bhd (Taman Impian Emas); Infra Park Sdn Bhd (MLIMA Kiara); KEB Berhad (Residensi Cove @ Kota Syahbandar); Matrix Concepts (Levia Residence Puchong); OCR Templer Sdn Bhd (D’Templer Hilltop Residences); Peter’s Group (Cherita Residences); Puncak Concept Sdn Bhd (Puncak LakePark City @ Cyberjaya); R&F Development Sdn Bhd (R&F Princess Cove); Steadfast Properties (Laguna Residences); Tiram Industrial Park Sdn Bhd (Akasia Business Park); Tropicana Corporation Berhad (Clarissa Serviced Suites, Tropicana Cenang); UEM Sunrise Berhad (Intrika, Serene Heightshase s); and Worldwide Holdings Berhad (Pavonia Worldwide, Bukit Bandaraya Shah Alam). Outstanding real estate figures The 13th PropertyGuru Asia Awards Malaysia with iProperty celebrated some of the impactful figures in Malaysian real estate. Tan Sri Dato’ Seri Dr. Jeffrey Cheah KBE AO, founder and chairman of Sunway Group, received the Life Achievement Award. Dato’ Seri Azmir Merican, group managing director and chief executive officer of Sime Darby Property, was named Real Estate Personality of the Year. Dato’ Sri Edwin Tan Pei Seng, executive chairman of Paragon Globe Berhad, was honoured as Rising Star, while Ms. Maggie Ng Mui Kit, chief executive officer of Kuok Group Property Division (Southern), received the Woman Changemaker Award. Consumers, catalysts, and consistency The Consumer Demand Award continued this year, recognising the property that captured the strongest genuine interest from Malaysian property seekers. Determined by consumer views and leads across PropertyGuru.com.my and iProperty.com.my, Leisure Farm Resort by Mulpha International was named Most In-Demand Bungalow/Villa, in addition to winning Best Resort-Style Township Development. The People’s Choice Awards also continued the tradition of tapping consumer opinion to identify the nation’s 10 favourite developers. This year, 15,383 votes were cast for developers that consumers in Malaysia admire and trust. The winners of the People’s Choice Awards in 2026 are: Berinda Group; Coronade Properties Sdn Bhd; CPI Land; Gunung Impian Development Sdn Bhd; JLand Group; KEB Berhad; Matrix Concepts; Pinnacle Group; Tropicana Corporation Berhad; and UEM Sunrise Berhad. In addition, PropertyGuru.com.my and iProperty.com.my presented several titles for the first time this year. IIB Experience Centre (IIBEX) by Iskandar Investment Berhad received the inaugural Real Estate Ecosystem Catalyst Award. The Consistency Excellence Awards also made their debut, recognising companies with consecutive years of wins at the awards. Gunung Impian Development Sdn Bhd won the 4-Year Consistency Excellence Award. Meanwhile, the 3-Year Consistency Excellence Awards were presented to Armani Group; Astaka Padu Sdn Bhd; Berinda Group; Coronade Properties Sdn Bhd; Iskandar Investment Berhad; JLand Group; R&F Development Sdn Bhd; and Tropicana Corporation Berhad. Live selection process Winners of the competitive categories were selected during the Live Judging Days from 30 June to 2 July 2026 at the Amari Hotel Kuala Lumpur. The evaluation process, independently supervised by HLB Ler Lum Chew, saw a multi-disciplinary panel from Malaysia’s leading professional bodies assess an expanded lineup of categories. This year’s panel was chaired by Datuk Ar. Ezumi Harzani Ismail, president of the Malaysian Institute of Architects (PAM) from 2020 to 2022, and included Ir. Ashwin Thurairajah, executive director, GreenRE Sdn Bhd; YBrs. Sr. Haji Ishak Ismail, president, Malaysian Institute of Property & Facility Managers (MIPFM) 2023–2027; Ms. Janice Chin, senior director, Capital Markets, JLL Appraisal & Property Services Sdn Bhd; Prof. Dr. Ir. Jeffrey Chiang Choong Luin, president, The Institution of Engineers Malaysia (IEM) 2024–2026; Dato’ Sr. Lau Wai Seang, president, Royal Institution of Surveyors Malaysia (RISM) 2017–2018; TPr. Mazrina Dato’ Abdul Khalid, president, Malaysian Institute of Planners (MIP) 2025–2027; Assoc. Prof. LAr. Dr. Nor Atiah Ismail, president, Institute of Landscape Architects Malaysia (ILAM) 2024–2026; Adj. Prof. IDr. Norshafina Ibrahim, president, Malaysian Institute of Interior Designers (MIID) 2024–2026; Mr. Oliver Wee, president, Master Builders Association Malaysia (MBAM) 2024–2026; Ar. Sarly Adre Sarkum, chief executive officer, Green Building Index (GBI); Ar. Dr. Serina Hijjas, president, Malaysia Green Building Council (MGBC) 2023–2027; and Ms. Tan Hui Yin, partner, Tan Chap & Associates. Datuk Ar. Ezumi Harzani Ismail said: “Good design is the product of discipline, clarity of intent, and an understanding of how people inhabit space. What struck me most among this year’s winners was a shared design intelligence: sensitivity to context and climate, thoughtful handling of landscape and light, and a commitment to sustainability that goes beyond token gestures. From the elegant restraint of landed homes to the confident lines of high-rise towers, these projects show that Malaysian design has matured into something both internationally credible and distinctly our own. And with quality consistent across every tier, good design is not a privilege of the few but a standard we can deliver for all. On behalf of the judging panel, I congratulate every winner for raising the bar for Malaysian real estate.” Jules Kay, managing director of PropertyGuru Asia Property Awards and Events, said: “This year’s awardees share a commitment to thoughtful placemaking, sustainable design, and creating developments that enhance the way people live, work, and connect. From transformative township masterplans to beautifully crafted landed homes, this year’s winners show that excellence equals lasting value for communities. We are proud to celebrate developers that deliver value and quality to homebuyers. We also celebrate the individual leaders whose passion and foresight continue to inspire the industry. Together, these achievements set a benchmark for Malaysian real estate.” Winners may advance to the PropertyGuru Asia Property Awards Grand Final, recognising the Best in Asia on 11 December 2026 at The Athenee Hotel, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Bangkok. The PropertyGuru Asia Awards Malaysia with iProperty is supported in 2026 by platinum sponsor Lim Soh & Goonting Advocates & Solicitors; official portal partners PropertyGuru.com.my and iProperty.com; official ESG knowledge partners Green Building Index (GBI), GreenRE, and Malaysia Green Building Council (MGBC); official magazine Property Report by PropertyGuru; strategic media partner Out of Home Media; media partners The Grid Asia, The Iskandarian, The Malaysia Voice, Niaga Times, Penang Property Talk, and Top 10 of Malaysia; official AI photo experience partner Gump; and official supervisor HLB. For more information, email awards@propertyguru.com or visit the official website: AsiaPropertyAwards.com. COMPLETE LIST OF WINNERS DEVELOPER AWARDS
